question.problem:
Find the Laplace transform $Y(s)=L\{y(t)\}$ if 

$$
{y}^{′}+4y={u}_{\pi /3}(t)\cdot cos\,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3})\,,\,y(0)=0,
$$

where ${u}_{\pi /3}(t)=u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{3})$ is the unit step function.

You may make use of the following result:

$$
L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}},\,s>0
$$

$Y(s)=$
{{field-1}},$\,s>0$
question.worked_solution:
First, we take the Laplace transform of both sides and use the addition and scalar multiplication properties of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{′}+4y\} & =L\{{u}_{\pi /3}(t)\cdot cos\,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3})\} \\ L\{{y}^{′}\}+4L\{y\} & =L\{{u}_{\pi /3}(t)\cdot cos\,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3})\}\end{aligned}
$$

To calculate $L\{{y}^{′}\},$ we use the formula for the Laplace transform of a derivative and the initial condition $y(0)=0:$

$$
L\{{y}^{′}\}=sY(s)-y(0)=sY(s)
$$

To find the transform of the right-hand side, we note that the term 

$$
{u}_{\pi /3}(t)\cdot cos\,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3})
$$

is in the form $u(t-a)\cdot f(t)$ where $a=\frac{\pi }{3}$ and $f(t)=cos\,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3}).$ This can be interpreted as time-delayed sinusoidal forcing. 

Now, recall that the second shifting theorem (time-shifting property) states

$$
L\{u(t-a)\cdot f(t)\}={e}^{-as}\cdot L\{f(t+a)\}.
$$

  

So, by the second shifting theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{u\,(t-\frac{\pi }{3})\cdot cos\,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3})\} & ={e}^{-(\pi /3)s}\cdot L\{cos\,(2\,(t+\frac{\pi }{3})-\frac{2\pi }{3})\} \\  & ={e}^{-\pi s/3}\cdot L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\} \\  & ={e}^{-\pi s/3}\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}+4} \\  & =\frac{s{e}^{-\pi s/3}}{{s}^{2}+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute these back into our transformed differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{{y}^{′}\}+4L\{y\} & =L\{{u}_{\pi /3}(t)cos\,(2t-\frac{2\pi }{3})\} \\ sY(s)+4Y(s) & =\frac{s{e}^{-\pi s/3}}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ (s+4)Y(s) & =\frac{s{e}^{-\pi s/3}}{{s}^{2}+4} \\ Y(s) & =\frac{s{e}^{-\pi s/3}}{({s}^{2}+4)(s+4)}\end{aligned}
$$
